doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: Big band drumming and keeping the band listening
summary: He loves the freedom of big band drumming, life on the bus, and leaving out fills to keep the band alert.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Yeah. A different style. Yeah. For sure. I’ll tell you, big band drumming is a dream and it’s a shame that opportunities are so scarce now unless you go into the Army or the Air Force and play in a service band. Because I realized that every night, unlike the fifth trumpet player, I could approach a chart differently. I didn’t have to play the same fills all the time, unless it was something that was crucial to the arrangement. But I could leave things out. I could play more. I could play less. And so every night it was great because it really forced me, and the whole rhythm section for that matter, to really use our

imaginations. Because if you don’t use your imagination that’s when you get bored. And I mean you lived for those, you had 22 hours off and two hours on, you know? And you’d ride that damn stinking bus for hours just in anticipation of getting on the bandstand and going after it. And every night was a new experience. Sometimes good, sometimes not so good. But at any rate it was there. And that’s what — Woody loved that. There were times when I would deliberately leave out a big fill that I usually played and the band wouldn’t come in right after that because they were so dependent upon the fill. And Woody would just laugh his ass off because he knew that’s how you keep the band in line, keep them listening.
Yeah there was an early jazz writer, Whitney Balliett, I think he said, “Jazz is the sound of surprise.”
Yeah, exactly, yeah. So Woody was fine with that sort of thing.
